steps.name: prompt
steps.text: Write the introduction for a paper on training users of sEMG-based gesture classification with error-augmented feedback. Motivate sEMG for HCI, review co-adaptive learning and the motor learning view of feedback, and describe our experiment and hypothesis.

steps.name: partial_draft
steps.text:
Surface electromyography (sEMG) is a convenient sensor modality for human-computer interaction (HCI) applications. In the past two decades, research has tried to translate the electrical activity of muscle contraction into control commands for general use computing, prosthetic control and motor rehabilitation. Since there is more and more demand for interfaces that are intuitive and responsive, there is also more focus on sEMG-based gesture recognition.

Traditional approaches to sEMG-based gesture recognition assumed that the mapping between muscle activation and gestures is stationary, and they did not consider that the user can adapt their behavior based on feedback about how the gestures are classified. Co-adaptive learning algorithms that came up in the past decade were a big shift, because they see both human and machine learning as parts of one integrated system. One important finding of these approaches is that when the human gets continuous feedback about the mapping of muscle activation to gesture, they can increase the classification performance by adapting their behavior. These adaptations can lead to increased class separability and increased movement repeatability. But the relationship between adaptations in the feature space and classifier performance is complex. Real-time classifier performance was also found to increase even when there were no changes in the relative class distributions in the EMG feature space. Even though this relationship between feature space class distributions and classifier performance is complex, the influence of human learning on myoelectric gesture classification is still a compelling thing to investigate.

- Motor skill learning view
  - intrinsic feedback (sensory info) + augmented feedback (not readily accessible intrinsically)
  - knowledge of performance (movements, muscle activations) vs knowledge of results (outcomes)
  - myoelectric control: KR = classifier output; KP = descriptions of sEMG features
  - error augmentation, reward manipulation -> rate and retention of learning, behavioral variability
  - error-augmented feedback not tested for sEMG co-adaptation (to our knowledge)
- Our study
  - does modified feedback about class posterior probabilities affect myoelectric control performance
  - error-augmented knowledge of results: alter probabilities, diminish class differences, harder to exceed predefined decision threshold; soften towards uniform distribution
  - related to error augmentation / error amplification: hastens learning, better self-evaluation, more retention
  - hypothesis: softening -> better subsequent classification via enhanced human skill learning
  - applications: prosthetics, assistive devices, HCI with brief 4-minute calibration

steps.name: rough_draft
steps.text:
Surface electromyography (sEMG) is a convenient sensor modality for human-computer interaction (HCI) applications. In the past two decades, research has tried to translate the electrical activity of muscle contraction into control commands for general use computing, prosthetic control and motor rehabilitation. Since there is more and more demand for interfaces that are intuitive and responsive, there is also more focus on sEMG-based gesture recognition.

Traditional approaches to sEMG-based gesture recognition assumed that the mapping between muscle activation and gestures is stationary, and they did not consider that the user can adapt their behavior based on feedback about how the gestures are classified. Co-adaptive learning algorithms that came up in the past decade were a big shift, because they see both human and machine learning as parts of one integrated system. One important finding of these approaches is that when the human gets continuous feedback about the mapping of muscle activation to gesture, they can increase the classification performance by adapting their behavior. These adaptations can lead to increased class separability and increased movement repeatability. But the relationship between adaptations in the feature space and classifier performance is complex. Real-time classifier performance was also found to increase even when there were no changes in the relative class distributions in the EMG feature space. Even though this relationship between feature space class distributions and classifier performance is complex, the influence of human learning on myoelectric gesture classification is still a compelling thing to investigate.

Human learning about myoelectric gesture classification can be seen as a kind of motor skill learning. In the motor learning literature, the canonical view is that humans use a combination of intrinsic feedback (sensory information) and augmented feedback (information that is not readily accessible through intrinsic feedback). Augmented feedback can again be split into 'knowledge of performance' (information about specific movements and muscle activations) or 'knowledge of results' (information about outcomes). In this study we focus on myoelectric control, where giving knowledge of results means giving the output of a classifier, and knowledge of performance means descriptions of the features that are extracted from the sEMG. It is well established that augmented feedback can shape human behavior in traditional motor skill learning settings. Strategies like error augmentation and reward manipulation were shown to affect the rate and the retention of learning and also behavioral variability. But as far as we know, error-augmented feedback has not been tested for co-adaptation approaches to sEMG-based gesture recognition.

In this study we did an experiment to test if modified feedback about class posterior probabilities affects performance in a myoelectric control task. We gave subjects a form of error-augmented knowledge of results: by altering the class probabilities we made the differences between classes smaller, which made it harder for the target gesture class to go over a predefined decision threshold. Specifically, we softened the probabilities towards a uniform distribution. This kind of feedback manipulation is closely related to earlier uses of error augmentation, which is also called error amplification. As said above, this kind of feedback was shown to hasten learning and improve the quality of self-evaluation and to increase retention of learned skills. So we hypothesized that error amplification by softening probabilities would increase the gesture classification performance afterwards by enhancing human skill learning. What we learn from this investigation could be applied broadly in myoelectric prosthetics, assistive devices and human-computer interfaces where users do only a brief 4-minute calibration and where human learning may be critical for the model performance to succeed.

steps.name: revised_draft
steps.text:
Surface electromyography (sEMG) provides a convenient sensor modality for human-computer interaction (HCI) applications [1]. In the past two decades, research efforts have sought to translate the electrical activity associated with muscle contraction into control commands for general use computing, prosthetic control, and motor rehabilitation [2,3]. As the demand for more intuitive and responsive interfaces has grown, the focus on sEMG-based gesture recognition has intensified.

Traditional approaches to sEMG-based gesture recognition assumed that the mapping between muscle activation and gestures was stationary, and did not consider the user's ability to adapt their behavior based on feedback about gesture classification performance. The emergence of co-adaptive learning algorithms in the past decade marked a shift, acknowledging both human and machine learning as parts of an integrated system [4,5,6,7,8,9]. One key finding from these approaches is that when the human receives continuous feedback about the mapping of muscle activation to gesture, they can increase classification performance through behavioral adaptations [10,11]. These adaptations can result in increased class separability [12] and increased movement repeatability [13]. However, the relationship between feature space adaptations and classifier performance is complex. Increased real-time classifier performance has also been found even without changes in relative class distributions in the EMG feature space [14]. Despite this complex relationship between feature space class distributions and classifier performance, the influence of human learning on myoelectric gesture classification remains a compelling target of investigation.

Human learning about myoelectric gesture classification can be considered a form of motor skill learning. In the motor learning literature, the canonical view is that humans use a combination of intrinsic feedback (sensory information) and augmented feedback (information that is not readily accessible through intrinsic feedback) [15]. Augmented feedback can be further categorized as providing 'knowledge of performance' (information about specific movements and muscle activations) or 'knowledge of results' (information about outcomes) [16,17]. In the present study, we focus on myoelectric control, where providing knowledge of results corresponds to providing output from a classifier, while knowledge of performance corresponds to descriptions of the features extracted from the sEMG. The ability to shape human behavior in traditional motor skill learning settings through augmented feedback is well established. Strategies such as error augmentation [18,19,20] and reward manipulation [21,22] have been shown to affect the rate and retention of learning as well as behavioral variability. Yet, to our knowledge, error-augmented feedback has not been tested for co-adaptation approaches to sEMG-based gesture recognition.

In this study, we conducted an experiment to test whether modified feedback about class posterior probabilities affects performance in a myoelectric control task. We provided subjects with a form of error-augmented knowledge of results: by altering class probabilities, we diminished the differences between classes, making it harder for the target gesture class to exceed a predefined decision threshold. In particular, we softened probabilities towards a uniform distribution. This form of feedback manipulation is closely related to previous uses of error augmentation, also called error amplification [23,24,25]. As mentioned, this form of feedback has been shown to hasten learning and improve the quality of self-evaluation [18,26] and to increase retention of learned skills [27,23]. We therefore hypothesized that error amplification by softening probabilities would increase subsequent gesture classification performance by enhancing human skill learning. The knowledge gained from this investigation has broad potential applications in myoelectric prosthetics, assistive devices, and human-computer interfaces where users perform only a brief 4-minute calibration and human learning may be critical to the success of model performance.
